rows.description: A child who is sad or shy tends to hunch and look down, and slumped sitting can reinforce the feeling. Playful movement, stretching and standing tall can lift energy a little.

rows.subtype: Long study sessions and body aches [Actor]
rows.description: A student sitting for hours feels back, neck and shoulder pain that adds to fatigue and irritability. Short walks, stretching and changes of position ease both body and mood.

rows.subtype: Desk-bound worker feeling stiff and low [Actor]
rows.description: A professional at a desk all day gets tight shoulders, headaches and sluggish thoughts, and blames stress alone. Small movement breaks and adjusting the workspace lift energy without big changes.

rows.subtype: Writing what is in the head [Actor]
rows.description: A schoolchild writes answers assuming the reader already knows the story, leaving out steps that seem obvious to them. Taking the reader's viewpoint is a skill that takes years to become automatic.
A teenager uses long words and stretched sentences to seem intelligent and ends up hard to follow. Clear writing feels less impressive to the writer but is far better for the reader.

rows.subtype: Email that says too little or too much [Actor]
rows.description: A student or intern writes an email with no clear request, or a long wall of text with the ask buried at the end. Readers skim, so the purpose and requested action should come in the first lines.
A toddler hides behind a parent, looks away or goes quiet with strangers. Shyness is a temperament trait and improves with gentle warm-up time, not pushing.
A child humiliated by failure may hide, go silent or say they are stupid. Shame targets the self, so adults separate the person from the act and offer safety.
A young adult listens, sits with a distressed friend and avoids quick fixes or judging. Support can be more useful than advice, and serious risk means involving professional help.
A child hides behind a parent at a party, whispers answers and joins play only after watching. Wants friends but needs time; pushing to say hello often deepens the freeze.

A teenager avoids answering in class, skips events and rehearses sentences for hours because of a strong fear of embarrassment. It differs from shyness in intensity and avoidance that shrinks life, and calls for support.
A young adult is quiet with strangers, enjoys small groups and does not suffer much about it. Being reserved is a temperament, not a problem to fix, and depth in a few friendships can be a strength.
A toddler talks over others because turn-taking is not yet formed, not because of rudeness. Adults model brief pauses and say your turn, my turn to build the habit.
A preschooler learns that conversation involves waiting; silence after a question may mean thinking, shyness or not understanding. A wise adult counts to five before rephrasing.
A child avoids telling a parent about a low grade or a quarrel and delays until it grows. Avoidance makes the eventual talk harder, and a calm parent makes the first admission easier.
A teenager in a serious conversation with a parent feels heat, cannot think, and blurts or shuts down. When the body is flooded, pausing and resuming later works better than pushing through.
